title: The Sun appears to move: sunlight and shadows from morning to evening

summary.text: A patch of sunlight on the floor creeps slowly across the room, even when nobody touches the window. In this unit your child marks a sun patch every 5 minutes and watches it move. They count their own shadow in footsteps in the morning, at noon and in the evening, and find it long, then short, then long again. They learn that the Sun rises in the east, is highest around noon and sets in the west. And they learn that the Sun only appears to move, because the Earth, with our home on it, is turning.
summary.art: A girl of 7 kneeling on a tiled floor beside a bright patch of sunlight from a balcony door, putting a coin at its corner, with a ginger cat asleep in the patch.

intro.hook: In the morning, your shadow on the road is longer than you are. At lunchtime it hides near your feet. Why does it change?
intro.text: Your body stayed the same size all day. Your shadow did not. A shadow is the dark patch where your body blocks the sunlight. So if the shadow changed, something about the sunlight changed. In this unit we watch the sunlight and the shadows from morning to evening. We find out how the Sun seems to move across the sky, and why.
intro.art: Two pictures side by side: a girl walking to school in the early morning with a very long shadow, and the same girl at lunchtime with a tiny shadow round her feet.

outcomes: By the end I can say how the Sun appears to move across the sky: it rises in the east, is highest around noon, and sets in the west.
By the end I can say that the Sun only seems to move round us, because the Earth turns.
By the end I can say that shadows are long in the morning and in the evening, and shortest around noon.
By the end I can say that a shadow points away from the Sun, so morning and evening shadows point opposite ways.
By the end I can mark how a sun patch or a shadow moves, and count how far it went.
By the end I can find which side of the sky the Sun is on from a shadow, without ever looking at the Sun.

terms.meaning: Sunrise is the time in the morning when the Sun first appears at the edge of the sky.
terms.example: At sunrise, the sky near the ground turns pink and orange, and the birds start calling.
terms.art: The Sun just peeping over a row of rooftops and a temple tower, with a pink sky.

terms.meaning: Sunset is the time in the evening when the Sun goes down below the edge of the sky.
terms.example: After sunset, the street lights come on and the sky slowly gets dark.
terms.art: An orange Sun half hidden behind coconut trees at the edge of the sky.

terms.meaning: Noon, or midday, is the middle of the day, when the Sun is highest in the sky.
terms.example: Around noon, your shadow is shorter than at any other time of the day.
terms.art: A child standing in a sunny school yard at noon, with a small shadow round her feet.

terms.meaning: A shadow is the darker patch where light cannot reach, because something is in the way.
terms.example: Under a neem tree on a sunny day, there is a cool shadow on the ground.
terms.art: A neem tree in sunshine with a dark round shadow on the ground under it.

terms.meaning: East is the side of the sky where the Sun rises in the morning.
terms.example: If the morning sunlight comes in through your bedroom window, that window looks east.
terms.art: A window with morning sunlight streaming in and a small label saying East.

terms.meaning: West is the side of the sky where the Sun sets in the evening. It is opposite east.
terms.example: If the evening sunlight comes into your kitchen, the kitchen window looks west.
terms.art: A kitchen window with orange evening sunlight and a small label saying West.

terms.meaning: Something appears to happen when it looks as if it happens, even if the real reason is different.
terms.example: From a moving train, the trees appear to rush backwards. Really, the train is moving.
terms.art: A child looking out of a train window at trees that look blurred and streaming backwards.

terms.meaning: To rotate means to spin or turn round. The Earth rotates once every day.
terms.example: A top rotates on the floor. The Earth rotates too, but so smoothly that we do not notice it.
terms.art: A spinning wooden top on a floor beside a small globe with a curved arrow round it.

terms.meaning: A sun patch is the bright shape that sunlight makes on a floor or wall when it comes in through a window or a door.
terms.example: In the morning, a cat often lies in the sun patch by the balcony door.
terms.art: A bright rectangle of sunlight on a tiled floor, with the dark stripes of a window grill across it.

terms.meaning: A sundial is a clock that tells the time from the shadow made by the Sun.
terms.example: At Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, a huge stone sundial shows the time with the shadow of a tall wall.
terms.art: A simple round sundial in a garden with a pointed shadow falling across the hour marks.

explanations.concept: The Sun appears to move across the sky
explanations.context: This card is about the path the Sun seems to take each day.
explanations.definition: Each day the Sun appears to rise in the east, climb higher until about noon, then sink lower and set in the west.
explanations.description: In the early morning, the Sun is low in the east. Through the morning it seems to climb, and around noon it is highest. In the afternoon it seems to sink, and in the evening it sets in the west. We can see all this from sunlight and shadows, without looking at the Sun.
examples: Early morning: the Sun is low, and the light comes in sideways through east windows.
Noon: the Sun is high, and the light falls almost straight down.
Evening: the Sun is low again, and the light comes in sideways through west windows.
explanations.art: A curved path of five small Suns over a row of buildings, low on the left labelled East, highest in the middle labelled Noon, and low on the right labelled West.

explanations.concept: Why the Sun seems to move: the Earth turns
explanations.context: This card answers the question from the sun patch test: what made the patch move?
explanations.definition: The Sun seems to move across our sky because the Earth rotates, or turns, once every day.
explanations.description: The Earth is a huge ball, and it is always turning. Our home, our street and we ourselves turn with it. As we turn, the Sun seems to rise, cross the sky and set. It is like sitting in a train: the trees seem to rush past, but really the train is moving. The turning is so smooth that we cannot feel it.
examples: From a moving train, still trees appear to move backwards.
On a turning merry-go-round, the people standing outside seem to slide past you.
The sun patch on your floor moved, though nobody touched the window.
explanations.art: A child on a merry-go-round seeing her mother standing still outside, with a small inset of the Earth turning in front of the Sun.

explanations.context: This card is about the Shadow Footsteps test, where you counted your own shadow at three times of day.
explanations.definition: When the Sun is low, shadows are long. When the Sun is high, shadows are short. So shadows are long in the morning and evening, and shortest around noon.
explanations.description: Sunlight travels in straight lines. When the Sun is low, its light comes in sideways, so your body blocks a long stretch of ground and your shadow is long. When the Sun is high, the light comes from above, so your shadow is short. Around noon it is shortest.
examples: At 8 in the morning, a child's shadow can be 10 or more of her own footsteps long.
Around noon, the same child's shadow may be only 1 or 2 footsteps long.
In the evening, the shadow is long again.
explanations.art: Three drawings of the same girl: morning with a long shadow, noon with a short shadow, evening with a long shadow pointing the other way, and a small Sun in each.

explanations.concept: A shadow points away from the Sun
explanations.context: This card is about which way your shadow points at different times of day.
explanations.definition: A shadow always falls on the side of a thing away from the light. So a shadow points away from the Sun.
explanations.description: A shadow falls on the side away from the Sun. In the morning the Sun is in the east, so shadows point west. In the evening the Sun is in the west, so shadows point east. So a shadow tells you where the Sun is, without looking at it. In most of India, for most of the year, the noon shadow is short and points a little to the north.
examples: Morning: the shadow of a lamp post points west.
Evening: the same shadow points east.
If your shadow is in front of you, the Sun is behind you.
explanations.art: A lamp post seen from above, with a morning shadow pointing one way, an evening shadow pointing the other way, and a small Sun on the far side of each.

explanations.concept: Noon with no shadow: Zero Shadow Day
explanations.context: This card is about a special day when, in some Indian cities, your noon shadow hides right under your feet.
explanations.definition: On Zero Shadow Day, the noon Sun is straight overhead, so an upright thing makes almost no shadow at its side.
explanations.description: At noon the Sun is usually a little to one side, so even then there is a small shadow. But south of a line called the Tropic of Cancer, the Sun is straight overhead at noon on two days each year. Then a standing pole or tumbler has almost no shadow beside it. Bengaluru has these days in late April and mid-August. Delhi is north of the line, so it never has one.
examples: In Bengaluru, people stand bottles and glasses on the ground at noon in late April to see their shadows vanish.
Chennai, Hyderabad, Mumbai and Kochi have Zero Shadow Days too, each on its own dates.
Delhi and Jaipur never have one.
explanations.art: A steel tumbler standing upright on a sunny terrace at noon, with no shadow beside it, only a thin dark ring at its base.

explanations.concept: Other beings follow the Sun's movement too
explanations.context: This card is about animals and plants that keep track of where the Sun is going, like the cat in the story.
explanations.definition: Many animals and plants keep track of the Sun's movement across the sky and use it.
explanations.description: Honeybees use the Sun to find their way back to flowers, and change direction as it moves. Young sunflower plants turn to face the Sun in the morning and follow it west. At night they turn back to face east. Cats move from patch to patch to stay in the warm sunshine. These beings sense the Sun, remember where it was, and get ready for where it will be.
examples: A honeybee finds her way home by the Sun, even as it moves.
A young sunflower plant faces east before sunrise.
A cat moves to the next sun patch as the first one slides away.

perspectives.explanation: Bees and sunflowers keep track of the Sun with an inner clock, and they sense, remember and act on what they sense.
Some scientists call these automatic responses, and prefer not to use words like remember and plan for plants.

explanations.art: A honeybee flying past a young sunflower plant that is facing the morning Sun, and a ginger cat lying in a sun patch by a window.

agreed.text: The Sun appears to rise in the east, cross the sky and set in the west every day.
agreed.evidence: People all over the world, in every age, have seen this. You can see it from your own sun patches and shadows.

agreed.text: The Sun seems to move because the Earth rotates once a day.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have shown the Earth's turning with swinging pendulums, with spacecraft photos and with the way the stars all circle round the sky at night.

agreed.text: Shadows are longest when the Sun is low, and shortest around noon, when the Sun is highest.
agreed.evidence: You can count your own shadow in footsteps at three times of day. Sundials have worked this way for thousands of years.

agreed.text: Never look straight at the Sun, because its light can hurt the back of your eyes.
agreed.evidence: Eye doctors see damage from looking at the Sun, often after people watch an eclipse without safe glasses.

challenging.claim: The Sun travels round the Earth once every day.
challenging.who: Most people for thousands of years, and the first idea of most children
challenging.for: It really does look that way. The Sun rises, crosses the sky and sets, and the ground does not seem to move.
challenging.against: The Earth turns once a day, and that makes the Sun seem to move. Swinging pendulums, photos from space, and the way all the stars wheel across the night sky together show it.
challenging.context: This card is about the oldest idea about the Sun's path.

challenging.claim: At noon, there is no shadow at all.
challenging.for: At noon, shadows are very short and hide close to your feet.
challenging.against: In most places, the noon Sun is a little to one side, so there is still a small shadow. Only on Zero Shadow Day, in places south of the Tropic of Cancer, is it straight overhead.
challenging.context: This card is about noon shadows.

challenging.claim: The Sun rises in exactly the same spot every day.
challenging.for: Every morning, the Sun rises on the east side of the sky.
challenging.against: Over the months, the place where the Sun rises slides slowly north and then back south along the edge of the sky. It rises exactly in the east only around 21 March and 23 September.
challenging.context: This card is about where the Sun rises.

big_questions.q: You were sitting still, yet the Earth was carrying you along. What does it really mean to be still?
big_questions.hint: Still compared with what? The floor, the Sun, or the whole sky?

big_questions.q: From the ground, the Sun moves. From space, the Earth turns. Is one of these more true than the other?
big_questions.hint: Both describe the same day. Which one explains more things at once?

big_questions.q: Why don't we notice the Earth turning, when it carries us so fast?
big_questions.hint: Think about a smooth train ride with your eyes closed.

big_questions.q: Long ago, people told the time from shadows. Now we use clocks. What else could you tell from the Sun if you watched it every day?
big_questions.hint: Think of seasons, directions and sleep.

big_questions.q: A cat knows where the next sun patch will be. How might she know?
big_questions.hint: Has she watched it before? Does she feel the warmth moving?

story.title: Kutti Follows the Sunshine
story.note: A made-up story. It is true that a sun patch moves across a floor during the day, that families in India dry chillies, vadam and mango slices in the sun and move them as the sunshine moves, and that cats seek out warm sunny spots.
text: Meenakshi lived on the third floor of a building in Madurai. She lived with her Amma, her little brother Hari and her grandmother, Ammamma. They also had a ginger cat called Kutti. Kutti loved one thing even more than fish. She loved lying in the sunshine.

On Saturday morning, a bright patch of sunlight lay on the floor by the balcony door. It had the shape of the door, with dark stripes from the grill. Kutti was curled up right in the middle of it, warm and sleepy.
Ammamma was out on the balcony, spreading red chillies on an old cotton saree to dry. "The sunshine is on this end now," she said. "I will move them after lunch."
Meenakshi sat down to draw. Hari played with his cars. After a while, Meenakshi looked up. Kutti had moved. She was lying a little closer to the door now, still right in the sunshine.
"Kutti moved the sunshine," said Hari. "She pulled it with her."
Meenakshi was not sure. "Let us find out," she said. She took a one-rupee coin and put it on the floor, right at one corner of the sun patch.
Then she lifted Kutti gently and carried her to the sofa. Kutti gave a cross little mew, turned round twice and went back to sleep.
Meenakshi and Hari watched the coin. At first, nothing happened. Hari counted to a hundred, twice. Then he shouted, "Look! The corner has moved away from the coin!"
It had. The bright corner was now a finger's width away from the coin. Kutti was on the sofa, far away. Nobody had touched the door or the curtain.
"So Kutti did not move it," said Meenakshi. "The sunshine moves by itself. Kutti just follows it to stay warm."
"Then what moves it?" asked Hari.

Ammamma came in from the balcony. "Come and see," she said. "But never look at the Sun. Look at the shadow of the water tank on the next building." Early that morning, the tank's shadow had stretched right across the terrace. Now it was much shorter.

"When I was your age," said Ammamma, "my mother dried mango slices on our roof. She moved them three times a day. In the morning, the sunshine came from one side. At noon, it was everywhere, and the shadows were tiny. In the evening, it came from the other side."
"Because the Sun moves across the sky," said Hari.

"It looks that way," said Ammamma. "The Sun seems to move. But really, the Earth is turning, slowly, all day long. Our building turns with it, and so do we. So the sunlight comes in through our door at a new slant, and the patch slides across the floor."
Hari stood very still in the middle of the room. "I am not moving," he said.
Meenakshi laughed. "You are," she said. "The coin showed it. The whole room is turning, and you are in it."

After lunch, Ammamma moved her chillies to the other end of the balcony. By the evening, the patch by the balcony door was gone. A new, long patch of orange light lay across the kitchen floor. It came in through the window on the other side of the flat.
Kutti was already lying in the new patch.
"How did she know it would be there?" asked Hari.
"She has been watching the sunshine move every day of her life," said Meenakshi. "She remembers where it goes."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Hari first thinks the cat pulls the sunshine with her. Meenakshi's coin test shows the patch moves even when the cat is far away. Ammamma explains that the Sun only seems to move, because the Earth, with the building on it, is turning.
ask: How did Meenakshi find out that Kutti was not moving the sunshine?
Why did Ammamma move her chillies after lunch?
Why was the water tank's shadow shorter later in the morning?
Why was the evening sunshine in the kitchen, and not by the balcony door?

games.title: Morning, Noon or Evening? Shadow clue cards
games.context: This is a card game about shadows. Each card describes a shadow. You must say whether it is morning, noon or evening, and give a reason.

printables.title: 12 clue cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

items.f: Your shadow is very long and points west.
items.b: Morning. The Sun is low in the east, so the shadow is long and points the other way, west.

items.f: Your shadow is tiny and hides round your feet.
items.b: Noon. The Sun is high, so the shadow is short.

items.f: Your shadow is very long and points east.
items.b: Evening. The Sun is low in the west, so the shadow points east.

items.f: The sunlight comes in sideways through the east window.
items.b: Morning. The Sun is low on the east side.

items.f: The coconut tree's shadow is a small dark circle under the tree.
items.b: Noon. The Sun is nearly overhead.

items.f: The orange sunlight comes in through the west window.
items.b: Evening. The Sun is low on the west side.

items.f: The shadow of the water tank stretches right across the terrace, towards the west.
items.b: Morning. A long shadow pointing west means a low Sun in the east.

items.f: Your shadow walks in front of you as you walk east.
items.b: Evening. The Sun is behind you, in the west, so your shadow is in front.

items.f: You must stand under the umbrella's middle to stay in its shade.
items.b: Noon. The Sun is high, so the shade is just under the umbrella.

items.f: The building's long shadow covers the whole road, on the east side.
items.b: Evening. The Sun is low in the west, so the shadow falls to the east.

items.f: A grandmother puts her chillies out where the first sunshine of the day reaches the balcony.
items.b: Morning. The first sunshine of the day comes from the east.

items.f: A bottle on the terrace has almost no shadow at all, in Bengaluru, in late April.
items.b: Noon, on Zero Shadow Day. The Sun is straight overhead.

rules: Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
The first player takes the top card and reads it aloud, or a grown-up reads it.
The player says morning, noon or evening.
Then they give a reason. Turn the card over to check.
1 point for the right time. 1 more point for a good reason.
Take turns until the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Mix them and put them face down.
flow.say: Each card tells you about a shadow or some sunshine. You must work out the time of day.
flow.kid: Each card is a shadow clue. Work out the time of day.

flow.do: 1. Players take turns to read a card and answer. 2. Ask for a reason every time. 3. Keep the score.
flow.say: Is it morning, noon or evening? How do you know?
flow.kid: Read the card. Morning, noon or evening? How do you know?
flow.parent: The reasons matter more than the guesses. Listen for: long means low Sun, short means high Sun, and the shadow points away from the Sun.

flow.do: Add up the points.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why?

check.q: A card says: your shadow is very long and points east. What time is it?
check.why: A long shadow means a low Sun. It points east, so the Sun is in the west. A low Sun in the west means evening.

rules: Tape the EAST sign on one wall and the WEST sign on the opposite wall. For the game, pretend these walls are east and west. Clear a space on the floor.
Play in pairs. One player stands in the middle of the room as the person. The other is the shadow. With 2 players, that is the whole game. With 4 players, two pairs take turns while the others watch.
The person turns over the top time card, looks at the front only, and holds the paper Sun from activity a5 (or a yellow plate) in the right place for that time.
The shadow player lies or curls on the floor from the person's feet, the right length and pointing the right way. At midnight, the shadow player hides.
The person reads the back of the card aloud. If the shadow is right, the pair gets 1 point.
Swap jobs after every two cards. The game ends when all 8 cards are used. With 2 players, try to get all 8 right together. With 4 players, the pair with more points wins.

flow.say: One of you stands. The other is the shadow: lie on the floor with your feet touching your partner's feet.
flow.kid: One of you stands. One of you is the shadow, on the floor.
flow.parent: Clear the floor first, so nobody bumps into furniture.

flow.do: 1. The person turns over a time card and holds the paper Sun in the right place. 2. The shadow player moves. 3. Read the back to check.
flow.say: Eight in the morning! The Sun is here, low by East. Shadow, where do you go? How long are you?
flow.kid: Look where the Sun is. Lie the right way. Long or short?

ask.q: Why did the shadow curl up at noon?
good: Because the Sun is high, so the shadow is short.
The light comes from above.

flow.do: Count the points. Then ask the question.
flow.say: Which time made the longest shadow? Which made none?
flow.kid: Which time made the longest shadow?

check.q: The caller shows the card for 4 in the afternoon. Which way should the shadow player lie?

experiments.title: The Moving Sun Patch: does sunlight on the floor stay still?
experiments.context: In this experiment you mark the corner of a patch of sunlight on your floor every 5 minutes. You find out whether the sunlight stays still, and if it moves, which way and how far.
experiments.question: If nobody touches the window or the curtain, does a patch of sunlight on the floor stay in the same place?
experiments.predict: Guess first. In 20 minutes, will the sun patch stay still, or move? If it moves, which way will it go? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Nobody touches the window, the door or the curtain during the test. We always mark the same corner of the patch. We mark it every 5 minutes by the clock, so the gaps are the same. The same child's fingers count the finger widths.
results_table: Finger widths from the first mark

materials.item: a window or balcony door that lets sunlight fall on the floor or a wall right now
5 coins, or 5 small paper strips with numbers 1 to 5 written on them
a clock or a phone to tell the time
a pencil and paper for the table

experiments.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Look only at the patch of light on the floor.

schedule.what: Guess, mark the corner of the sun patch five times, 5 minutes apart, then count how far it moved.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the patch with five small numbered dots at its corner, from mark 1 to mark 5.

setup.art: A bright rectangle of sunlight with grill stripes on a tiled floor, coming in through a balcony door.
setup.caption: 1. Find a patch of sunlight on the floor.

setup.art: A child's hand putting a coin labelled 1 exactly at one sharp corner of the sun patch.
setup.caption: 2. Put coin 1 at one corner. Write down the time.

setup.art: Five coins in a short line on the floor, with the corner of the sun patch now next to coin 5 and a little way from coin 1.
setup.caption: 3. Every 5 minutes, put the next coin at the same corner.

setup.caption: 4. Count the finger widths from coin 1 to coin 5.

flow.do: 1. Find a sun patch on the floor, or on a wall. 2. Pick one corner of the patch that has a sharp edge. 3. Ask your child for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Look at this patch of sunlight. Nobody will touch the window. In 20 minutes, will the patch stay here, or move? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the patch of sunlight. Will it stay still, or move? Why do you think so?

good: It will stay, because the window is not moving.
It will move, because the Sun moves.
It will move a little, because the shadows change in the day.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good start. Do not explain anything yet. If a curtain makes the edge fuzzy, use the sharp shadow of one grill bar or the window frame instead.

flow.do: 1. Put coin 1 exactly at the corner. 2. Write the time and mark 1 in the table.
flow.say: Put this coin right at the corner of the patch. What is the time now? Write it next to mark 1.
flow.kid: Put coin 1 right at the corner. Tell your grown-up the time to write down.

flow.do: 1. Every 5 minutes, your child puts the next coin at the same corner. 2. Write the time each time. 3. While you wait, read the story Kutti Follows the Sunshine aloud, or draw the patch.
flow.say: Five minutes have passed. Where is the corner now? Put the next coin there. Is it in the same place as before?
flow.kid: Every 5 minutes, put the next coin at the corner. Is it moving?

ask.q: Which way is the corner moving?
good: Towards the window.
Away from the window.
Sideways, towards the wall.
It is going the same way each time.

flow.parent: The corner usually moves a finger width or more every 5 minutes. In the morning, the patch often moves towards the window and gets smaller. In the afternoon, it often moves away from the window and gets longer. Any steady movement is the real result.

flow.do: 1. Count the finger widths from coin 1 to coin 5. 2. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Count the finger widths from the first coin to the last. Nobody touched the window. So what made the patch move?
flow.kid: Count the fingers from coin 1 to coin 5. What made the patch move?

ask.q: What do you think, and what did you see?
good: The patch moved, even though nobody touched the window.
It moved the same way every time.
The sunlight is coming in at a new slant, because the Sun seems to move.

check.q: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 2, marks a sun patch every 5 minutes. Nobody touches the window. What will she see?
options: The patch moves a little each time
The patch stays exactly where it was
The patch jumps to the other side of the room
check.why: The Sun seems to move slowly across the sky, so the sunlight comes in at a new slant. The patch creeps a little way every few minutes. It does not jump.

flow.parent: Let your child give a reason before you explain. Then read the card about why the Sun seems to move: the Earth, with your home on it, is turning.

experiments.title: Shadow Footsteps: how long is your shadow in the morning, at noon and in the evening? (on a sunny terrace or in the building compound)
experiments.context: In this experiment you stand in the same sunny spot three times in one day. Each time, you count how many of your own footsteps long your shadow is, and see which way it points.
experiments.question: Is your shadow the same length all day, or does it change between morning, noon and evening?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When will your shadow be longest: in the morning, at noon or in the evening? When will it be shortest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We stand on the same spot each time, with our back straight and our arms down. We count in the same child's footsteps, heel touching toe.

materials.item: a flat, sunny open place such as a terrace, the building compound or a quiet lane, on a sunny day
a piece of chalk, or a small stone or leaf, to mark the spot where you stand
a clock or a phone
the results table on paper

experiments.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. A grown-up comes along to the terrace or the compound. At noon in summer, keep each visit short, wear a cap and drink water.

schedule.what: Count your shadow at about 8 in the morning, around noon and at about 5 in the evening, about 5 minutes each time. Then compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, and draw yourself three times with your shadow, the right length and pointing the right way.

setup.art: A girl standing on a chalk cross on a sunny terrace in the morning, with a long shadow stretching away from her.
setup.caption: 1. Stand on your mark. Keep still.

setup.art: A grown-up putting a stone at the end of the girl's long shadow, while the girl watches from her chalk cross.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up marks the end of your shadow with a stone. Walk from your cross to the stone, heel to toe, and count.

setup.art: The same girl on the same mark at noon with a tiny shadow round her feet.
setup.caption: 3. Come back at noon and in the evening. Count again.

flow.do: 1. Draw the results table. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason for each time of day.
flow.say: We will count your shadow three times today: morning, noon and evening. When will it be longest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: When will your shadow be longest? Morning, noon or evening? Why?
flow.parent: This test needs an open sunny place. A grown-up fills in the table. If you have no open sunny place, skip this test or do it at a park or on a relative's terrace.

flow.do: 1. At about 8 in the morning, mark a spot with chalk. 2. Your child stands on it. 3. Put a stone where the shadow of the head ends. 4. Your child walks heel to toe from the cross to the stone and counts. 5. Note a building or tree the shadow points at.
flow.say: Stand on the cross and keep still. I will put a stone where your shadow ends. Now walk from the cross to the stone, heel to toe, and count. What is the shadow pointing at?
flow.kid: Stand on the cross. Keep still. Then walk to the stone, heel to toe, and count your steps.
flow.parent: A child's shadow at 8 in the morning is often 8 to 15 of the child's own footsteps. The exact number depends on the month and the city.

flow.do: 1. Go back around noon, when your shadow looks shortest (about 12 to 12:30 in most of India, earlier in the east). 2. Your child stands on the same cross. 3. Mark the end of the shadow with a stone and count again.
flow.say: It is around noon now. Before we count, guess: longer or shorter than this morning?
flow.kid: It is noon. Guess first. Then count your shadow again.
flow.parent: Around noon the shadow is only 0 to 3 footsteps, close round the feet. In the summer months in South India, it can almost vanish.

flow.do: 1. Go back at about 5 in the evening. 2. Your child stands on the same cross. 3. Mark the end of the shadow with a stone, count again and see which way the shadow points.
flow.say: It is evening. Count your shadow. Which way does it point now? Is that the same way as this morning?
flow.kid: It is evening. Count your shadow. Which way does it point now?

ask.q: What is different about the evening shadow?
good: It is long again.
It points the other way from the morning shadow.
It points towards the east now.

flow.parent: The evening shadow points nearly the opposite way from the morning one, because the Sun is now on the other side of the sky.
flow.wait: Come back at about 5 in the evening

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask what your child thinks, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Your body was the same height all day. What changed your shadow?
flow.kid: You did not grow or shrink. So why did your shadow change?

check.q: Rani, a girl in Class 2, finds her shadow is 12 footsteps long in the morning. What is it likely to be at noon?
check.why: At noon the Sun is high, so the light comes from above and the shadow is short. A shadow of 12 or 25 footsteps would need a low Sun.

activities.title: Sunny Rooms: where is the sunlight coming in now?
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and find every place where sunlight is coming in. Later in the day you check again, to see if the sunshine has changed rooms.

materials.item: your home, on a sunny day
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: In the morning, find every room with sunlight coming in, and draw a quick map.
In the afternoon, check every room again and mark the map.

activities.record: A simple map of your home with a yellow sun beside each room that had sunlight in the morning, and an orange sun for the afternoon.

setup.art: A simple child's map of a flat with boxes for rooms: kitchen, bedroom, hall, balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a box for each room.

setup.art: A child standing at a bedroom doorway, pointing at a bright patch of sunlight on the bed.
setup.caption: 2. Walk round. Where is sunlight coming in?

setup.art: The same map with yellow suns by the balcony and bedroom, and orange suns by the kitchen.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the map in the morning and again in the afternoon.

flow.do: 1. Help your child draw a box for each room. 2. Write the room names.
flow.say: Let us draw our home. One box for each room.
flow.kid: Draw a box for each room in your home.

flow.do: 1. Walk round every room together. 2. Look for sun patches on floors, walls and beds. 3. Your child draws a yellow sun on each sunny room.
flow.say: Let us find every place where sunlight is coming in. Look at the floors and the walls. Do not look at the Sun itself.
flow.kid: Find every room with sunlight in it. Draw a yellow sun there.

ask.q: Which rooms have sunlight now? Why only those?
good: The balcony and the bedroom, because their windows face the Sun.
Rooms on one side of the flat.

flow.do: 1. In the afternoon, walk round again. 2. Your child draws an orange sun in each sunny room. 3. Compare the two times.
flow.say: It is afternoon now. Guess first: will the sunshine be in the same rooms as this morning? Now let us check.
flow.kid: Guess first. Is the sunshine in the same rooms now? Go and check.

check.q: Ishaan, a boy in Class 2, lives in a flat where morning sunlight comes in through the bedroom window. Where is the evening sunlight most likely to come in?
options: A window on the other side of the flat
No window, because the Sun has gone
check.why: In the morning the Sun is in the east. In the evening it is in the west, on the other side. So the evening sunshine comes in through windows on the other side of the flat.

flow.parent: If your home gets no direct sunlight, look at the building opposite instead: which side of it is lit in the morning, and which in the afternoon?

activities.title: Find East and West from Your Home
activities.context: In this activity you use the morning and evening sunshine to work out which side of your home is east and which is west. Then you put up two signs.

materials.item: two sheets of paper and a pen
cellotape
your Sunny Rooms map, if you made one

schedule.what: Decide which side is east and which is west, and put up the two signs.

activities.record: Two signs on your walls, East and West, and a sentence: The Sun rises over ___ and sets over ___.

setup.art: A child writing EAST on one sheet of paper and WEST on another.
setup.caption: 1. Make two signs: East and West.

setup.art: The East sign taped on the wall by the window where morning sunlight comes in, and the West sign on the opposite wall.
setup.caption: 2. Tape East where the morning Sun comes in, and West on the opposite side.

flow.do: 1. Look at the Sunny Rooms map, or remember where the morning sunlight comes in. 2. Ask your child which side the Sun rises on.
flow.say: The Sun rises in the east. Where does the morning sunshine come into our home? So which side is east?
flow.kid: Where does the morning sunshine come in? That side is east.
flow.parent: If you do this in the evening, find where the evening sunshine comes in: that side is west, and the opposite side is east.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes EAST and WEST on two sheets. 2. Tape East on the wall on the morning side, and West on the wall opposite.
flow.say: Put the East sign where the morning Sun comes in. Where should the West sign go?
flow.kid: Tape up the East sign. West goes on the opposite side.

flow.do: Look out of the east window together. Name what the Sun rises behind: a building, a hill, a tree or a water tank.
flow.say: The Sun rises over there, behind something. What is it? Do not look at the Sun. Look early in the morning, or at the buildings.
flow.kid: What does the Sun rise behind? A building? A tree? Say it.

check.q: Farhan, a boy in Class 2, puts his East sign on his bedroom wall. Where should his West sign go?
check.why: West is opposite east. The Sun rises on the east side and sets on the opposite side, the west.

flow.parent: Sunrise is roughly east, not exactly. Over the year, it slides a little north and south. Roughly east is all your child needs.

activities.title: Draw the Sun's Path from Your Window
activities.context: In this activity you draw the view from one window or the balcony, and mark where the Sun is at three times of day. You use the brightness and the shadows to find it, never by looking at the Sun.

materials.item: paper and crayons, with yellow
a window or balcony with a wide view of the buildings and sky
a clock

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Use the shadows to find where it is.

schedule.what: Draw the view and mark the Sun's place in the morning.
Mark it again in the afternoon, and join the three suns with a curved line.

activities.record: A drawing of your view with three yellow suns, each with its time, joined by a curved arrow.

setup.art: A child drawing the row of buildings and a water tank seen from a balcony, along the bottom of a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Draw what you see along the bottom: buildings, trees, tanks.

setup.art: The drawing with three small yellow suns, low on the left, high in the middle and lower on the right, joined by a curved arrow, each with a time.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the Sun three times. Join the suns with a curve.

flow.do: 1. Choose a window or the balcony. 2. Your child draws the buildings, trees and tanks along the bottom of the paper.
flow.say: Draw what you can see from here, along the bottom of the page. Draw the tall things carefully.
flow.kid: Draw what you see along the bottom of the page.

flow.do: 1. Stand with your child at the window. 2. Look at the buildings and the shadows. 3. The Sun is on the side away from the shadows. 4. Your child draws a small sun there and writes the time.
flow.say: Do not look at the Sun. Look at the buildings and the shadows. The Sun is on the side away from the shadows. Draw a small sun there.
flow.kid: Do not look at the Sun. Find the shadows. The Sun is on the other side. Draw a sun there.

flow.do: 1. Come back around noon and in the afternoon. 2. Mark the Sun each time. 3. Join the three suns with a curved arrow.
flow.say: Before you draw, guess: will the Sun be higher or lower than this morning? Now draw it. Join your suns with a curve.
flow.kid: Guess first. Higher or lower? Draw the new sun. Join the suns.

check.q: Tanvi, a girl in Class 2, drew the Sun at 9 in the morning and at noon. Where will her 3 o'clock sun go?
options: Lower down, on the other side from the morning sun
In the same place as the morning sun
check.why: After noon, the Sun seems to sink again, towards the west. So at 3 o'clock it is lower than at noon, on the opposite side from the morning sun.

flow.wait: Come back around noon, then in the afternoon
flow.parent: Around noon in most of India, the Sun is very high, so draw it near the top of the paper. Do not lean over the balcony railing to look up. The pattern is low, high, low.

activities.title: Who Follows the Sun at Home? Ask the family
activities.context: In this activity you ask the grown-ups at home and in your building how they use the Sun's movement. Many families already move their drying clothes, chillies or pickles as the sunshine moves.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
two or three grown-ups to ask: family, a neighbour or the building watchman

schedule.what: Ask three questions to two or three grown-ups, and write or draw their answers.

activities.record: A small table: who you asked, what they dry or keep in the sun, and when they move it.

setup.art: A girl with a notebook asking a grown-up a question on a balcony, with clothes drying on a stand.
setup.caption: 1. Ask a grown-up your three questions.

setup.art: A notebook page with a small table: names, things dried in the sun, and times such as morning and after lunch.
setup.caption: 2. Write or draw the answers in a table.

flow.do: Read the three questions with your child: What do you dry in the sun? Where do you put it? Do you move it during the day, and when?
flow.say: We are going to ask grown-ups how they use the sunshine. Here are three questions. Which one will you ask first?
flow.kid: Ask three questions. What do you dry? Where? Do you move it?

flow.do: 1. Your child asks two or three grown-ups. 2. You help write short answers in the table.
flow.say: Ask the first grown-up. Listen carefully. Then we will write the answer.
flow.kid: Ask your questions. Listen. Then help write the answers.
flow.parent: Common answers are washing on a stand, chillies, papad, vadam, mango slices for pickle, rice for a few days, and bedding. Many people move them once or twice a day, as the sunshine moves along the balcony or the terrace.

flow.do: Ask your child what all the answers have in common.
flow.say: Why do people need to move their drying things? What does that tell us about the sunshine?
flow.kid: Why do people move their drying things?

good: Because the sunshine moves to another place.
Because the Sun seems to move across the sky, so the shadows move too.

check.q: Selvi, a woman who lives in a flat, puts her washing in a sunny corner of the terrace at 9 in the morning. At 3 in the afternoon, the corner is in shade. Why?
options: The Sun has moved across the sky, so the shadows have moved
The terrace moved away from the building
check.why: As the Sun seems to move from east to west, the shadows of walls and tanks swing round. A corner that was sunny in the morning can be in shade by the afternoon.

activities.title: The Sun on a Stick: show the path from sunrise to sunset
activities.context: In this activity you make a paper Sun on a stick and show its path across a wall, from your East sign to your West sign, while a grown-up calls out times of the day.

materials.item: a paper plate or a round of yellow paper
a pencil, ruler or ice-cream stick for a handle
cellotape and crayons
your East and West signs, or two sheets marked E and W

schedule.what: Make the paper Sun, then move it to the right place for each time called out.

activities.record: A drawing of the arch your Sun travelled, with the times written along it.

setup.art: A yellow paper plate Sun taped to a ruler, held by a child.
setup.caption: 1. Make a Sun on a stick.

setup.art: A child holding the paper Sun high in the middle of a room, with an East sign low on one wall and a West sign low on the opposite wall.
setup.caption: 2. Move the Sun low from East, high in the middle, low to West.

flow.do: Your child colours the paper plate yellow and tapes it to the stick.
flow.say: Make your Sun. Colour it bright yellow.
flow.kid: Colour your Sun. Tape it to the stick.

flow.do: 1. Call out times in a mixed order: breakfast, sunrise, lunch, evening play, sunset, mid-morning. 2. Your child holds the Sun at the right place each time.
flow.say: Breakfast time! Where is the Sun? Now lunchtime! Now sunset! Show me.
flow.kid: Listen for the time. Hold the Sun in the right place.

ask.q: Where is the Sun at lunchtime?
good: High up, near the top.
Almost over my head.

flow.do: Ask your child where their own shadow would be for two of the times.
flow.say: If the Sun is here, low by the East sign, where would your shadow point?
flow.kid: The Sun is by the East sign. Where does your shadow point?

check.q: Meena, a girl in Class 2, holds her paper Sun low, near the West sign. What time of day is she showing?
check.why: The Sun sets in the west. Low near the West sign means it is evening, close to sunset.

projects.title: The Floor Clock: make a sun patch tell the time
projects.context: In this project you mark where a sun patch is every half hour on one sunny day, and label each mark with the time. The next day, you test your floor clock: does the patch reach each mark at the same time?

materials.item: a window or door that lets sunlight onto the floor for at least two hours
small strips of paper or masking tape, and a pen
a clock or phone

schedule.what: Every half hour for two hours, stick a strip at the same corner of the sun patch and write the time on it. Each mark takes about 2 minutes.
Without looking at a clock, guess the time from where the patch corner is. Then check the clock. Do it three or four times.

projects.record: A photo or drawing of the floor clock with its time strips, and a table: my guess from the floor clock, the real time.

setup.art: A row of small paper strips stuck on a tiled floor in a gentle curve, each with a time written on it: 9:00, 9:30, 10:00, 10:30.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: stick a time strip at the patch corner every half hour.

setup.art: A girl kneeling by the strips the next day, with the patch corner just touching the 10:00 strip, and a grown-up checking a phone clock.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: read the time from the patch. Check the clock.

flow.do: 1. Pick a sun patch that lasts at least two hours. 2. Choose one sharp corner. 3. Cut 5 strips.
flow.say: We are going to turn this sun patch into a clock. Which corner has the sharpest edge?
flow.kid: Pick the sharpest corner of the sun patch.

flow.do: 1. Stick the first strip at the corner and write the time. 2. Every half hour, stick the next strip at the corner and write the time. 3. Leave the strips in place.
flow.say: It is half past nine. Stick a strip at the corner and write the time.
flow.kid: Stick a strip at the corner. Write the time on it.
flow.wait: Every half hour for two hours

flow.do: 1. The next day, ask your child to read the time from the patch, without a clock. 2. Then check the clock together. 3. Do this three or four times.
flow.say: Look at the patch. Which strip is it touching? So what time do you think it is? Now let us check the clock.
flow.kid: Which strip is the corner touching? What time is it, then? Check the clock.
flow.parent: Do not move the furniture, the curtain or the strips overnight. If the next day is cloudy, wait for a sunny day.

flow.do: Ask your child how good the floor clock was.
flow.say: Was your floor clock right? Why does a sun patch work like a clock?
flow.kid: Was your floor clock right? Why does it work?

check.q: Leela, a girl in Class 2, made a floor clock. It worked on Monday and on Tuesday. Why can a sun patch tell the time?
options: The Sun seems to move across the sky the same way every day
The patch moves only when someone walks past
check.why: The Earth turns at the same speed every day, so the Sun seems to take the same path. The patch reaches each mark at nearly the same time each day.

flow.parent: Over a few weeks, the patch drifts a little, because the Sun's path changes with the seasons. Over two days, the floor clock is usually right to within a few minutes.

challenges.title: Shade for a Toy, All Day Long
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a shade for a small toy, so that it stays in shadow when a torch Sun shines low from one side, high from above, and low from the other side.
challenges.problem: Can you build a shade from card and paper that keeps a toy in shadow in the morning, at noon and in the evening?
constraints: Use only paper, card from old boxes, tape and ice-cream sticks or pencils.
The shade must not be a closed box. The toy must still be seen from the front.
Test it with a torch held low on the left, high above, and low on the right.
materials: card from an old box, paper and cellotape
a torch, in a dim room
general: A flat roof on four sticks shades the toy at noon, when the torch is high.
A roof alone fails in the morning and evening, because the low light comes in sideways under it.
Add walls on the two sides where the low morning and evening light comes from.
creative: Make the roof wide and slope it down at both sides, like the roof of a Kerala house.
Hang paper flaps from the roof edges that you can lower in the evening.
Use a tall tree made of card on one side, the way a real tree shades a house.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own shade. Test it at all three torch places. Where does light still sneak in? Change one thing and test again.

setup.art: A small toy elephant on a table with a torch held low on the left, and a card roof on four pencils above the toy.
setup.caption: 1. Build a shade over a toy.

setup.art: The torch held low from the left, then high above, then low from the right, with the toy's shadow checked each time.
setup.caption: 2. Test with the torch low, high and low again.

flow.do: Read the challenge with your child. Show the materials.
flow.say: The torch is the Sun. It will shine from low on this side, then from high up, then from low on the other side. How will you keep the toy in the shade every time?
flow.kid: The torch is the Sun. Keep the toy in the shade all day.

flow.do: 1. Let your child build. 2. Test the shade at all three torch places. 3. Help with tape.
flow.say: Test it now. Torch low on the left. Is the toy in shadow? Now high above. Now low on the right.
flow.kid: Test it. Low on the left. High above. Low on the right. Is the toy shaded?
flow.parent: Most first designs are a flat roof, which works only at noon. Let your child find this out by testing, before you give any hints.

flow.do: Ask your child which torch place was hardest, and why.
flow.say: Which Sun was hardest to block: morning, noon or evening? Why?
flow.kid: Which Sun was hardest to block? Why?

check.q: Divya, a girl in Class 2, puts a flat roof over her toy. When does the torch Sun still shine on the toy?
options: When the torch is low at one side
When the torch is high above
check.why: A low light comes in sideways, under the edge of the roof. A flat roof blocks light only from above, like the noon Sun.

quiz.p: On which side of the sky does the Sun set?
quiz.why: The Sun sets in the west every evening. It rises in the east, on the opposite side.

quiz.p: When is the Sun highest in the sky?
quiz.why: The Sun seems to climb through the morning, is highest around noon, and sinks in the afternoon.

quiz.p: Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky?
opts: The Earth turns once a day
The Sun runs round the Earth
The clouds push the Sun along
quiz.why: The Earth rotates, carrying us with it. From the ground, that makes the Sun seem to move. The Sun is not going round us.

quiz.p: Nila is on a train. The trees outside seem to rush backwards. What is really moving?
quiz.why: The train moves, so still things outside appear to move the other way. The turning Earth makes the Sun appear to move in the same way.

quiz.p: At what time of day is your shadow shortest?
quiz.why: Around noon the Sun is high, so its light comes from above and your body blocks only a small patch near your feet.

quiz.p: Why is your shadow long in the early morning?
opts: The Sun is low, so its light comes in sideways
You are taller in the morning
The Sun is closer in the morning
quiz.why: A low Sun shines sideways, so your body blocks the light over a long stretch of ground.

quiz.p: In the morning, the Sun is in the east. Which way do shadows point?
quiz.why: A shadow falls on the side away from the light. With the Sun in the east, shadows point west.

quiz.p: Your shadow is in front of you as you walk. Where is the Sun?
quiz.why: A shadow points away from the Sun. If your shadow is in front, the Sun must be behind you.

quiz.p: Pooja, a girl in Class 2, marked a sun patch corner every 5 minutes. The marks went further and further from the first one. What did she find?
opts: The sun patch moves slowly and steadily
The sun patch moves only when she looks away
quiz.why: Her marks show that the patch creeps a little way every few minutes, because the Sun seems to move across the sky.

quiz.p: What is the safe way to find where the Sun is?
opts: Look at a shadow. The Sun is on the opposite side
Look at the Sun for just a second
Look at the Sun through sunglasses
quiz.why: Looking at the Sun, even briefly or with sunglasses, can hurt the back of your eyes. A shadow tells you where the Sun is without any danger.

quiz.p: The shadow of a lamp post points towards the temple. Where is the Sun?
opts: On the side of the lamp post away from the temple
quiz.why: The Sun is always on the opposite side from the shadow. So it is on the side away from the temple.

worksheets.title: The Sun's path and our shadows (core)

items.p: On which side of the sky does the Sun rise?
items.why: The Sun rises in the east every morning. A strong answer can point to the east side of the home.

items.p: True or false: at noon, shadows are at their longest.
items.why: False. At noon the Sun is high, so shadows are at their shortest. They are longest in the early morning and the evening.

items.p: Draw a line from each time to the shadow it makes.
pairs: a short shadow near the feet
items.why: A low Sun makes a long shadow, and a high Sun a short one. The shadow points away from the Sun.

items.p: Draw yourself standing in the sunshine at noon. Draw your shadow too.
items.a: A child with a small dark shadow close round the feet, and the Sun high above.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the Sun high up and the shadow short and close to the feet.

items.p: When the Sun is low in the sky, a shadow is ___.
items.why: A low Sun shines sideways, so the shadow stretches a long way.

items.p: Put the Sun's places in order, from morning to evening.
items.why: The Sun seems to rise in the east, climb to its highest around noon, then sink and set in the west.

items.p: True or false: the shadow of a tree points towards the Sun.
items.why: False. A shadow falls on the side away from the Sun, so it points away from the Sun.

items.p: Remember the Moving Sun Patch test. Say it, and a grown-up writes it down: what happened to the corner of the patch?
items.a: The corner moved a little further from the first coin every 5 minutes, though nobody touched the window.
items.why: A strong answer says the patch moved by itself and steadily, and names the way it went.

items.p: Label the picture: sunrise, noon, sunset, east, west.
a: sunrise: the low Sun on the left
noon: the high Sun in the middle
sunset: the low Sun on the right
east: the left edge of the sky
west: the right edge of the sky
items.why: These are the main places on the Sun's daily path.
items.art: A curved path of three Suns over a row of buildings: low on the left, high in the middle, low on the right, with blank label boxes.

items.p: Sort these into: safe ways to find the Sun, and not safe.
items: looking at the Sun through sunglasses
feeling which cheek is warm, with eyes closed
staring at the Sun for one second
seeing which wall is brightly lit
items.why: Sunlight is strong enough to hurt the back of the eye, even through sunglasses. Shadows, warmth and lit walls show where the Sun is without looking at it.

worksheets.title: The Sun's path and our shadows (stretch)

items.p: Gauri, a girl in Class 2, sees that her shadow points west and is very long. Is it morning or evening?
items.why: A shadow points away from the Sun. Pointing west means the Sun is in the east, low down. A low Sun in the east means morning.

items.p: Three friends are arguing about the Sun's path.

views.says: The Sun moves across the sky. I can see it with my own eyes, by the shadows.
The Earth turns. The Sun only seems to move, like trees from a train.
From the ground, you cannot tell which one is moving. Both ways describe the same day.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason from your own tests. Then say one thing another friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence. Kavya is right about what we see. Nila is right about why: the Earth turns. Arjun is right that we cannot tell it from the ground.
items.why: Scientists agree the Earth turns, and that explains the sky most simply. But from the ground, the Sun really does appear to move. Each friend sees part of it.

items.p: True or false: if you sit very still on the floor, you are not moving at all.
items.why: False. The Earth turns all the time and carries you, your home and the floor with it. The moving sun patch shows it.

items.p: Draw a tree and the tree's shadow in the morning. Then draw the same tree and the shadow in the evening. Draw the Sun each time.
items.a: Two trees: in one, the Sun is low on one side and the long shadow points the other way. In the other, the Sun and shadow have swapped sides.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the Sun low both times, makes both shadows long, and points each shadow away from its Sun.

items.p: Which is the odd one out? Sunrise, noon, sunset, midnight.
items.why: At midnight the Sun is not in our sky at all. At sunrise, noon and sunset, we can see sunshine.

items.p: The Earth turns round once every ___.
items.why: The Earth rotates once a day. That is why the Sun comes back to the same place in the sky each day.

items.p: Label the picture of a flat: east window, west window, morning sun patch, evening sun patch.
a: east window: on the side where the Sun rises
west window: on the opposite side
morning sun patch: on the floor near the east window
evening sun patch: on the floor near the west window
items.why: Morning sunlight comes in through east windows and evening sunlight through west windows, so the patches are on opposite sides.
items.art: A simple plan of a flat with a window on the left and a window on the right, and two blank label boxes near each.

items.p: A shadow always points ___ from the Sun.
items.why: Light cannot get through the thing in the way, so the dark patch falls on the side away from the Sun.

items.p: Sort these times into: long shadow, and short shadow.
items.why: The lower the Sun, the longer the shadow. Early morning and evening are long, and around noon is short.

items.p: Put these parts of the story Kutti Follows the Sunshine in order.
items: The bright corner has moved away from the coin.
Meenakshi carries Kutti to the sofa.
Meenakshi puts a coin at the corner of the sun patch.
a: Meenakshi puts a coin at the corner of the sun patch.
Meenakshi carries Kutti to the sofa.
The bright corner has moved away from the coin.
items.why: The coin marks the corner first. Then Kutti is moved away, and the corner still moves, so Kutti did not move it.

worksheets.title: The Sun's path and our shadows (challenge)

items.p: Many people think the Sun goes round the Earth, because that is what it looks like. What would you show a friend to help them think again? You can say it and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: For example: a train ride, where still trees seem to move because we are moving. Or the sun patch, which moved though nothing in the room moved.
items.why: A strong answer uses something the friend can see or try, and explains that something moving can make still things seem to move.

items.p: In Bengaluru, on a day in late April, a girl stands in the sun at noon. Her shadow hides right under her feet. Why?
opts: The Sun has gone behind a cloud
items.why: On Zero Shadow Day, the noon Sun is straight overhead. The light falls straight down, so the shadow is right under her.

items.p: Sneha, a girl in Class 2, wants to dry her clothes in the sun all afternoon. Her balcony faces east. Is it a good place?
opts: No, an east balcony gets the morning sun, not the afternoon sun
Yes, an east balcony is sunny all day
Yes, because the Sun sets in the east
items.why: The Sun is in the east in the morning. In the afternoon it is in the west, so a west-facing place gets the afternoon sun.

items.p: Put these shadows of the same girl in order, from shortest to longest: at 7 in the morning, at 10 in the morning, at noon.
items.why: The higher the Sun, the shorter the shadow. The Sun is highest at noon, a bit lower at 10, and lowest at 7.

items.p: True or false: the Sun rises at the same moment everywhere in India.
items.why: False. The Earth turns towards the east, so places in the east see the Sun first. In Arunachal Pradesh, the Sun rises almost two hours before it does in the far west of Gujarat.

items.p: Design a shade for a bench on a terrace that keeps it shady in the morning and in the evening, not only at noon. Draw it, with the Sun.
items.a: A roof with walls or a screen on the east and west sides, or a very wide roof that comes down low on both sides.
items.why: A strong design blocks the low morning Sun from the east and the low evening Sun from the west, not only the high noon Sun.

items.p: Two friends, Sunita and Imran, disagree about when noon is.

views.says: Noon is when the clock says 12 o'clock.
Noon is when the shadows are shortest, because the Sun is highest.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. Sunita is right that clocks call 12 o'clock noon, so everyone shares one time. Imran is right that the Sun's noon is when shadows are shortest. In many Indian cities that is a little after or a little before 12.
items.why: Clock noon and Sun noon are not exactly the same. All of India uses one clock time, but the Sun is highest at slightly different times in different cities.

items.p: Draw a line from each being to how they use the Sun's movement.
pairs: finds her way back to the flowers by the Sun
turns to follow the Sun, and faces east before sunrise
moves to the next sun patch to stay warm
items.why: Many beings keep track of where the Sun is going and act on it, each in their own way.

items.p: Bengaluru has 2 Zero Shadow Days every year. How many Zero Shadow Days is that in 5 years?
items.why: Count in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. That is 10 Zero Shadow Days.

items.p: True or false: the Sun sets exactly in the west every day of the year.
items.why: False. The Sun sets exactly in the west only around 21 March and 23 September. On other days it sets a little north or south of west.

applications: Sundials, like the giant Samrat Yantra at Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, tell the time from the shadow of the Sun.
Families across India dry chillies, papad, vadam, mango slices and washing in the sun, and move them as the sunshine moves.
Architects place windows, balconies and sunshades so rooms get gentle morning light and stay cooler in the hot afternoon.
Solar panels are tilted to face the part of the sky where the Sun spends most of the day. Some big ones turn slowly to follow the Sun.
Hikers and sailors have used the Sun's place in the sky to find east and west.

open_questions.q: Why does the Earth's turning speed up and slow down by tiny amounts?
open_questions.why_open: Clocks show that some days are a few thousandths of a second shorter or longer than others. Scientists think the Moon, the oceans, the air and the Earth's melted core all play a part, but they still argue about how much each one matters.

open_questions.q: Were the great stone wheels of the Konark Sun Temple in Odisha made to tell the time?
open_questions.why_open: Guides show visitors how to read the time from the shadows on the wheels' spokes. But no old record says the builders meant them as sundials, so historians are not sure.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a young sunflower plant know when to turn back east at night?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have shown that an inner clock helps, and that the two sides of the stem grow at different times. How the clock and the growing work together is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the Moving Sun Patch test, Leela, a girl in Class 2, found that her patch corner moved 3 finger widths in 15 minutes. If it keeps going at the same speed, how far will it move in 30 minutes?
maths.explain: 30 minutes is two lots of 15 minutes. Each lot moves the corner 3 finger widths. 3 and 3 make 6.
maths.context: This is about the Moving Sun Patch test, where you marked a corner of sunlight every 5 minutes.
maths.why_maths: Because the patch moves at a steady speed, we can use equal groups to predict where it will be later.

maths.problem: In the Shadow Footsteps test, Rani, a girl in Class 2, counted her shadow. It was 11 footsteps in the morning, 2 at noon and 14 in the evening. Which shadow was longest? How many footsteps longer was it than the morning shadow?
maths.answer: The evening shadow was longest. It was 3 footsteps longer than the morning shadow.
maths.explain: 14 is more than 11, and both are more than 2. Count on from 11 to 14: 12, 13, 14. That is 3 more.
maths.context: This is about the Shadow Footsteps test, where you counted your shadow three times in one day.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the numbers shows the pattern at a glance: long, short, long.

maths.problem: In the story, Meenakshi's grandmother Ammamma moves her drying chillies at 8 o'clock in the morning, at 12 o'clock, and at 4 o'clock in the afternoon. How many hours are there between each move?
maths.explain: From 8 o'clock to 12 o'clock: 9, 10, 11, 12. That is 4 hours. From 12 o'clock to 4 o'clock: 1, 2, 3, 4. That is 4 hours too.
maths.context: This is about the activity where you asked the family how they follow the sunshine.
maths.why_maths: Counting the hours shows that the sunshine moves along the balcony at a steady pace, so the moves can be planned.

maths.problem: Meenakshi, the girl in the story, marks a sun patch every 5 minutes. Her first mark is at 9:00, the next at 9:05, then 9:10. What time will her fifth mark be?
maths.explain: Count on in fives: 9:00, 9:05, 9:10, 9:15, 9:20. The fifth mark is at 9:20.
maths.context: This is about the Moving Sun Patch test, where you marked the corner every 5 minutes.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the pattern in the times lets you know when to make each mark without looking it up.

roots.context: We have watched a sun patch creep across the floor, and our own shadows change from morning to evening. Now we ask what the moving patch tells us about ourselves and our home.

deep_truth.truth: The sun patch crept across your floor while the window stayed where it was. The Sun does not travel round the Earth each day. The Earth turns, and it carries your home round with it. So even sitting still on the floor, you were moving the whole time.
deep_truth.habit: We call a thing still when it does not move compared with the things near it. The room, the floor and you were all moving together, so none of you could see it. Only the sunlight, coming from far outside, showed the movement.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Moving Sun Patch test, the corner of the patch moved a few finger widths from the first coin in 20 minutes. Nobody had touched the window, the curtain or the coins.

three.who_am_i: You are someone riding on a turning Earth. Even asleep in bed, you travel all the way round with it every day.
three.what_is_life: Cats, honeybees and young sunflower plants all keep track of where the Sun is going. Living beings watch the sky and plan by it, just as you can.
three.what_is_this_world: The ground under your feet is moving all the time. The Sun's daily journey across the sky is the Earth's own turn, seen from the ground.

roots.thread: One turning of the Earth makes the whole day. It brings the sunrise to Kohima first, and to Kochi a little later. It makes long morning shadows, short noon shadows and long evening shadows from the same Sun. Morning, noon and evening are not three different things. They are one movement, seen at different moments.

teachings.teaching: The Aitareya Brahmana, an old Sanskrit text, says the Sun never really rises or sets. It says that when people think the Sun is setting, it is only making night on one side and day on the other.
teachings.link: Your sun patch test agrees that rising and setting are not what they seem. The old text gave a different reason. We now know it is the Earth's turning that makes the Sun seem to rise and set.

teachings.teaching: Jain teachers say that a thing can be truly described in more than one way, depending on where you stand. They tell of blind men who each touch one part of an elephant and each describe the elephant differently.
teachings.link: From the ground, the Sun moves across the sky. From space, the Earth turns. Both describe the same day, from two places.

teachings.teaching: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,500 years ago, said you cannot step into the same river twice, because new water is always flowing past.
teachings.link: Your floor looked as still as a calm pond. Yet it was always moving with the Earth. Even things that look still are on the move.

science.text: The Earth turns once a day. In most of India, the ground carries you east at about 1,500 kilometres an hour, faster than a jet plane.
Young sunflower plants follow the Sun across the sky by day and turn back east at night. An inner clock helps them get ready for the sunrise.

other_view.view: Movement is always measured against something else. So from the ground, it is fair to say the Sun moves across the sky. Saying the Earth turns is chosen because it explains the Sun, the stars and the seasons together, most simply.

practice.title: Sit in the Sun Patch
practice.say: Sit at the edge of a sun patch, with your toes just touching its corner. Close your eyes. Feel the warmth on your toes. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly, ten times. Now open your eyes. Is the corner still touching your toes? You sat still. What moved?
practice.kid: Sit with your toes at the corner of the sun patch. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly ten times. Open your eyes. Where is the corner now?

ask: You sat still, yet the patch moved. What else around you might be moving that you do not notice?
From the ground the Sun moves, and from space the Earth turns. Which way of saying it feels true to you, and why?

how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, most people thought the Earth stood still and the Sun travelled round it once a day. It really does look that way. About 2,300 years ago, a Greek astronomer called Aristarchus of Samos said that the Earth turns, and also goes round the Sun. Seleucus, who lived in Seleucia on the river Tigris, in what is now Iraq, agreed with him. Almost nobody else did. About 1,500 years ago in India, Aryabhata wrote that the Earth turns. He said the stars only seem to move west, like still trees that seem to move backwards when you sit in a boat. In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus in Poland wrote a book with the Sun in the middle. Later, careful tests with telescopes and pendulums showed that the Earth really does turn. These thinkers were right, though most people around them did not believe it.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristarchus of Samos, a Greek astronomer; Seleucus of Seleucia, on the river Tigris; Aryabhata in India; later Nicolaus Copernicus in Poland
how_we_found_out.when: About 2,300 years ago for Aristarchus, about 2,150 years ago for Seleucus, about 1,500 years ago for Aryabhata, and 1543 for Copernicus
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the Earth stands still and the Sun travels round it every day. It looks that way from the ground, but later evidence from telescopes, pendulums and photos from space showed that the Earth turns.
how_we_found_out.art: An old Greek astronomer on an island hillside at sunset, pointing at the ground and drawing a turning circle in the sand, while others shake their heads.
